lesson_scope: Definite integrals and exact geometric area bounded by a curve and the x-axis, regions wholly above or wholly below the x-axis, finding bounds from intercepts, horizontal-line complements, splitting intervals across axis crossings, and solving for parameters from given bounded areas.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: basic evaluation of a linear definite integral with given numerical limits.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of evaluating limits on a definite integral [F(b) - F(a)].

hints: Find the antiderivative of $(2x + 1)$: $\int (2x + 1) \, dx = x^2 + x$.
Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value: $12 - 2 = 10$.

walkthrough.text:
Find the indefinite integral:
$$\int (2x + 1) \, dx = \left[x^2 + x\right]_1^3$$

Substitute the upper limit $x = 3$ and lower limit $x = 1$:
$$= \left((3)^2 + 3\right) - \left((1)^2 + 1\right)$$

Evaluate the arithmetic:
$$= (9 + 3) - (1 + 1) = 12 - 2 = 10$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: calculating area under a monomial curve y = 3x^2 above the x-axis.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of setting up area as definite integral.

hints: Since the curve is wholly above the $x$-axis on $[1, 2]$, the area is $\text{Area} = \int_1^2 3x^2 \, dx$.

walkthrough.text:
Set up the definite integral for area:
$$\text{Area} = \int_1^2 3x^2 \, dx$$

Integrate and apply limits:
$$= \left[x^3\right]_1^2 = (2)^3 - (1)^3 = 8 - 1 = 7 \text{ square units}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: area under square root curve from x = 0 to x = 4.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of integrating fractional powers over definite bounds.

hints: Write the area integral: $\text{Area} = \int_0^4 x^{1/2} \, dx$.

walkthrough.text:
Set up the area integral:
$$\text{Area} = \int_0^4 x^{1/2} \, dx$$

Apply the power rule to integrate:
$$= \left[\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_0^4$$

Evaluate at the limits:
$$= \frac{2}{3}(4)^{3/2} - 0 = \frac{2}{3}(8) = \frac{16}{3} \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Forms $\int_0^4 x^{1/2} \, dx$ and integrates to obtain $\left[\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_0^4$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: calculating geometric area for a region wholly below the x-axis taking absolute value of signed integral.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check that geometric area is the absolute value of a below-axis definite integral.

hints: The region is bounded between $x = 0$ (the $y$-axis) and $x = 2$.
Since area must be positive, take the absolute value: $\text{Area} = \left|-\dfrac{16}{3}\right| = \dfrac{16}{3}$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the definite integral over $[0, 2]$:
$$\int_0^2 (x^2 - 4) \, dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3} - 4x\right]_0^2$$

Substitute the limits:
$$= \left(\frac{2^3}{3} - 4(2)\right) - 0 = \frac{8}{3} - 8 = -\frac{16}{3}$$

Take the magnitude for geometric area:
$$\text{Area} = \left|-\frac{16}{3}\right| = \frac{16}{3} \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Evaluates signed integral as $-\frac{16}{3}$ and takes absolute value to obtain $\frac{16}{3}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: finding x-intercepts to identify integration limits and evaluating area of bounded quadratic loop.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of solving for roots to find integration limits.

hints: Find the $x$-intercepts by setting $y = 0$: $4x - x^2 = 0 \implies x(4 - x) = 0 \implies x = 0$ and $x = 4$.
Set up the area integral: $\text{Area} = \int_0^4 (4x - x^2) \, dx$.

walkthrough.text:
Find where the curve meets the $x$-axis:
$$4x - x^2 = 0 \implies x(4 - x) = 0 \implies x = 0, \; x = 4$$

Set up and evaluate the definite integral:
$$\text{Area} = \int_0^4 (4x - x^2) \, dx = \left[2x^2 - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^4$$

Substitute the limits:
$$= \left(2(4)^2 - \frac{4^3}{3}\right) - 0 = 32 - \frac{64}{3} = \frac{96 - 64}{3} = \frac{32}{3} \text{ square units}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: area under reciprocal squared curve 8/x^2.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of integrating negative index over bounds.

hints: Write the integrand using negative indices: $\text{Area} = \int_2^4 8x^{-2} \, dx$.

walkthrough.text:
Express the integrand in index form:
$$\text{Area} = \int_2^4 8x^{-2} \, dx$$

Integrate:
$$= \left[-\frac{8}{x}\right]_2^4$$

Evaluate at the limits:
$$= \left(-\frac{8}{4}\right) - \left(-\frac{8}{2}\right) = -2 - (-4) = -2 + 4 = 2 \text{ square units}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: evaluating definite integral of a three-term quadratic polynomial wholly above the x-axis.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires definite integral of polynomial over standard limits.

hints: Since $y = 3x^2 - 4x + 2$ lies above the $x$-axis, set up the area integral: $\text{Area} = \int_0^2 (3x^2 - 4x + 2) \, dx$.
Evaluate at $x = 2$: $2^3 - 2(2^2) + 2(2) = 8 - 8 + 4 = 4$. At $x = 0$, the value is $0$. Hence the area is $4$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Set up the definite integral for the area bounded between $x = 0$ and $x = 2$:
$$\text{Area} = \int_0^2 (3x^2 - 4x + 2) \, dx$$

Find the antiderivative:
$$= \left[x^3 - 2x^2 + 2x\right]_0^2$$

Evaluate the upper and lower limits:
$$= \left((2)^3 - 2(2)^2 + 2(2)\right) - \left((0)^3 - 2(0)^2 + 2(0)\right)$$
$$= (8 - 8 + 4) - 0 = 4 \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Evaluates the limits to obtain $4$ square units.

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: evaluating area between symmetric bounds for a curve wholly below the x-axis.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires geometric area calculation for below-axis region.

hints: Since the curve is wholly below the $x$-axis on $[-1, 1]$, the definite integral $\int_{-1}^1 (x^2 - 4) \, dx$ will yield a negative value.
State the geometric area as the positive magnitude: $\text{Area} = \dfrac{22}{3}$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Set up the definite integral:
$$\int_{-1}^1 (x^2 - 4) \, dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3} - 4x\right]_{-1}^1$$

Evaluate at upper and lower limits:
$$= \left(\frac{1}{3} - 4\right) - \left(-\frac{1}{3} - 4(-1)\right) = -\frac{11}{3} - \frac{11}{3} = -\frac{22}{3}$$

Take the absolute value for geometric area:
$$\text{Area} = \left|-\frac{22}{3}\right| = \frac{22}{3} \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Takes the magnitude and states $\frac{22}{3}$ square units.

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: definite integration involving reverse chain rule with fractional exponent over limits [0, 5].

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires definite integration of linear composite radical.

walkthrough.text:
Set up the definite integral for area:
$$\text{Area} = \int_0^5 \left(2(3x + 1)^{1/2} - 1\right) \, dx$$

Apply the reverse chain rule:
$$= \left[\frac{2(3x + 1)^{3/2}}{3 \times \frac{3}{2}} - x\right]_0^5 = \left[\frac{4}{9}(3x + 1)^{3/2} - x\right]_0^5$$

Substitute the limits:
$$= \left(\frac{4}{9}(16)^{3/2} - 5\right) - \left(\frac{4}{9}(1)^{3/2} - 0\right)$$
$$= \left(\frac{4 \times 64}{9} - 5\right) - \frac{4}{9} = \frac{256 - 4}{9} - 5 = \frac{252}{9} - 5 = 28 - 5 = 23 \text{ square units}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: finding intercept from radical equation and integrating to compute finite enclosed area.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires finding non-zero intercept of radical curve and evaluating definite integral.

hints: Set up the area integral from $x = 0$ to $x = 9$: $\int_0^9 (6x^{1/2} - 2x) \, dx$.

walkthrough.text:
Find the positive $x$-intercept $P$:
$$6\sqrt{x} - 2x = 0 \implies 2\sqrt{x}(3 - \sqrt{x}) = 0 \implies \sqrt{x} = 3 \implies x = 9$$

Integrate from $0$ to $9$:
$$\text{Area} = \int_0^9 (6x^{1/2} - 2x) \, dx = \left[4x^{3/2} - x^2\right]_0^9$$

Evaluate at limits:
$$= \left(4(9)^{3/2} - 9^2\right) - 0 = 4(27) - 81 = 108 - 81 = 27 \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Solves $6\sqrt{x}-2x=0$ to obtain the positive intercept $x=9$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: complementary area subtraction using bounding rectangle and curve integral.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires subtracting area under curve from enclosing rectangle.

hints: The area bounded between the curve, the line $y = 4$, and the $y$-axis is the area of the rectangle minus the area under the curve: $\text{Area} = 4(64) - \int_0^{64} x^{1/3} \, dx$.
Subtract from rectangle area $256$: $256 - 192 = 64$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Identify the bounding rectangle area with width $64$ and height $4$:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{rect}} = 64 \times 4 = 256$$

Subtract to obtain the desired region's area:
$$\text{Area} = 256 - 192 = 64 \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Evaluates the area under the curve as $\frac34(64)^{4/3}=192$.
Subtracts from $256$ to obtain $64$ square units.

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: splitting domain across x-axis crossings into above-axis and below-axis segments to determine total geometric area.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires splitting integral at x-axis intercepts to sum positive and negative regions.

hints: The curve crosses the $x$-axis at $x = -1$ and $x = 1$. Split the interval $[-2, 2]$ into three parts: $[-2, -1]$, $[-1, 1]$, and $[1, 2]$.

On $[-2, -1]$ and $[1, 2]$, the curve is above the axis. By symmetry, the area of each outer piece is $\int_1^2 (x^2 - 1) \, dx = \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} - x\right]_1^2 = \left(\dfrac{8}{3} - 2\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{3} - 1\right) = \dfrac{2}{3} - \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = \dfrac{4}{3}$.
On $[-1, 1]$, the curve is below the axis: $\left|\int_{-1}^1 (x^2 - 1) \, dx\right| = \left|\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} - x\right]_{-1}^1\right| = \left|-\dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac{2}{3}\right| = \dfrac{4}{3}$.
Sum the three areas: $\dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3} = 4$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Identify the signs of $y = x^2 - 1$ across $[-2, 2]$:
- Above axis for $x \in [-2, -1]$ and $x \in [1, 2]$
- Below axis for $x \in [-1, 1]$

Calculate the area of the outer regions:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{outer}} = 2 \int_1^2 (x^2 - 1) \, dx = 2\left[\frac{x^3}{3} - x\right]_1^2 = 2\left(\left(\frac{8}{3} - 2\right) - \left(\frac{1}{3} - 1\right)\right) = 2\left(\frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3}\right) = \frac{8}{3}$$

Calculate the magnitude of the central below-axis region:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{middle}} = \left|\int_{-1}^1 (x^2 - 1) \, dx\right| = \left|\left[\frac{x^3}{3} - x\right]_{-1}^1\right| = \left|-\frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3}\right| = \frac{4}{3}$$

Sum all positive regions:
$$\text{Total Area} = \frac{8}{3} + \frac{4}{3} = \frac{12}{3} = 4 \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Splits the interval at both intercepts $x=-1$ and $x=1$.
Finds the combined area of the two outer regions as $\frac83$.
Finds the magnitude of the central below-axis region as $\frac43$.
Adds the positive component areas to obtain $4$ square units.

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: parameterized intercept deduction followed by definite integral area expression and solving for constant k.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires factoring radical expression to find positive root in parameter k.

walkthrough.text:
Set $y = 0$ to find the $x$-intercepts:
$$k\sqrt{x} - x = 0$$
$$\sqrt{x}(k - \sqrt{x}) = 0$$

For the non-zero intercept:
$$k - \sqrt{x} = 0 \implies \sqrt{x} = k \implies x = k^2$$

ai_rubric.observable: Uses $k>0$ to obtain the positive intercept $x=k^2$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires evaluating parameterized area integral and solving for k.

walkthrough.text:
Set up the integral for the area under the curve from $0$ to $k^2$:
$$\text{Area} = \int_0^{k^2} (kx^{1/2} - x) \, dx$$

Integrate:
$$= \left[\frac{2k}{3}x^{3/2} - \frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^{k^2}$$

Equate to the given area $\frac{27}{2}$ and solve for $k$:
$$\frac{k^4}{6} = \frac{27}{2} \implies k^4 = 6 \times \frac{27}{2} = 81$$
$$\text{Since } k > 0, \quad k = 3$$

ai_rubric.observable: Simplifies the area to $\frac{k^4}{6}$ and equates it to $\frac{27}{2}$.
